preamble: The voiceless bilabial fricative [ɸ] becoming the labio-velar glide [w] involves both voicing and the loss of friction. The classic case is Japanese: by the 11th century, Early Middle Japanese medial /ɸ/ (from earlier *p) had merged with /w/ between vowels. This is why 'river' is written かは (kafa) in historical kana orthography but is pronounced kawa, and 'garden' and 'rock' are には, いは but niwa, iwa. Before /a/ the glide remained; before other vowels it was later lost or became [j] (iɸe > ije 'house'). Non-medial ɸ was not affected and later became [h]. No comparable regular case outside Japonic has been verified.

examples.note: Intervocalic ɸ merged with w by the 11th century; the historical spelling かは survived until the 1946 kana reform.

sources: Frellesvig, B. (2010). A History of the Japanese Language. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511778322
